---
title: "R11. Data ethics and personal data"
description: "The NHSBSA data ethics position, what to do when a question raises something, and personal data."
---

Analysis at NHSBSA uses data about people, and informs decisions that affect them. This page
carries the ethics position and the personal data obligations behind the questions Phase 1 asks.

## Data ethics

Analysis should be undertaken in line with legal and ethical obligations and any other relevant
public service codes of conduct.[^src-govs-010-principle-5]

The **Data and AI Ethics Framework** provides guidance on using data appropriately and responsibly
when planning, implementing and evaluating a policy or service.[^src-govs-010-section-6-1]

::: {.callout-note title="The framework was retitled and rescoped in December 2025" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
GovS 010 cites it as the **Data Ethics Framework**, which is the 2020 edition. On 18 December 2025 it
was retitled the **Data and AI Ethics Framework**, its scope was extended to AI and algorithmic
technologies, and four principles were added. Use the current framework, not the title GovS 010 names.

It publishes a **self-assessment tool**. Use that rather than a second instrument.
:::

Ethics is a design activity, not a compliance check at the end. The framework has seven principles,
and each one is a question worth asking before the work starts.

- **Transparency.** Could you explain to the people in the data what you did and why?
- **Accountability.** Who is answerable if this turns out to be wrong?
- **Fairness.** Could the analysis, or the decision it informs, affect some groups differently? Five
  questions turn that from open-ended into answerable. Who is **represented** in the data, and in
  what proportion? Who is **missing** from it altogether? Is any variable acting as a **proxy** for
  a protected or sensitive characteristic? Do **outcomes differ** across groups once you look? How
  much fairness work is **proportionate** to what this analysis decides? An exploratory count at
  Level 1 does not need a bias audit. A model that decides who is eligible for something does.
- **Privacy.** Is the data being used no more than the question requires? NHSBSA's Statistical Disclosure Control protocol is where this is already answered. [NHSBSA templates and documents](r2-templates-and-documents.qmd) lists the protocol with the other
  NHSBSA documents this playbook draws on. Follow them rather than this page: a disclosure control
  protocol summarised in a playbook is a protocol with two versions.
- **Environmental sustainability.** What does producing and running this analysis cost, and is that
  proportionate to what it is for? This matters most for repeated pipelines and for anything using
  large models.
- **Societal impact.** Who is affected by the decision this analysis informs, beyond the people in
  the data? This is a scoping question, so it belongs in
  [Phase 1, engagement and scoping](../01-engagement-and-scoping/index.qmd) as well
  as here.
- **Safety.** What harm could follow if this is wrong, misread, or used for something it was not
  built for?

The last two are the ones with no established NHSBSA route. Societal impact in particular is worth
raising at scoping rather than discovering at publication.

Accountability is often the most clarifying of the seven. If nobody can answer it, the governance is
not yet in place. See [roles and responsibilities](../06-roles/index.qmd).

## When a question raises something

Asking the seven questions is the easy half. The half that gets skipped is what happens when one of
them turns something up. An ethical concern with no record of what was decided about it is
indistinguishable, a year later, from one nobody noticed.

**Record six things.** They fit in a short block in the project record, and they are the same six
whether the concern is fairness, privacy, safety or societal impact.

| Field | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| **Affected groups** | Who is touched by this, in the data and beyond it |
| **Harms and benefits** | What could go wrong, and what the analysis is for. Both, because a harm recorded without the benefit beside it reads as a reason to stop rather than a thing to manage |
| **Mitigations** | What you actually changed: the method, the caveat, the scope, the publication decision |
| **Residual risk** | What is still there after the mitigations, stated plainly rather than implied by silence |
| **Accountable decision-maker** | The role that accepted that residual risk. Not the analyst, unless the analyst genuinely holds that authority |
| **Escalation route** | Where it went, if the analyst and the commissioner could not settle it between them |

**This is an audit trail, not an approval gate.** Most concerns are settled in the conversation that
raises them, and six lines in the project record is the whole of it. The block earns its keep on the
small number that are not settled, where the question a year later is not whether anybody worried but
what they decided and who agreed to it.

::: {.callout-note title="Where an ethical concern goes if it is not settled" appearance="minimal" icon=false}
<br>
A design and plan should cover escalation routes that let analysts and stakeholders raise
concerns.[^src-govs-010-section-5-3] Having them written down is the standard's expectation rather
than this playbook's preference, and which routes they are is NHSBSA's to settle.

**Proposed**, and consistent with the routes in
[roles and responsibilities](../06-roles/index.qmd): the commissioner decides first, because they
own the decision the analysis informs. Unresolved, it goes to the **Analytical Quality and Assurance
Lead**. Where the concern is about something that will be published as an official statistic, it goes
to the **Head of Profession for Statistics**, because that is already the route for whether an output
is fit to publish.

**Refusing to do a piece of analysis is a legitimate outcome of this route**, and it is not the
analyst's alone to take. That is what the accountable decision-maker field is for.
:::

## Personal data

Where personal data is used in analysis, this must be in accordance with NHSBSA policy and prevailing
legislation. That obligation comes from the legislation itself, not from this playbook and not from
GovS 010. The standard says the same in its own terms, that where personal data has been used this
should be in accordance with the organisation's policies and prevailing legislation.[^src-govs-010-section-6-14]

Where analysis using personal data is published, you may include in the publication:[^src-govs-010-section-6-14]

- when personal data has been used, and the justification for its use
- how guidance has been followed
- the steps taken to protect the data

Information and data should be classified and securely managed in line with GovS 007 Security. They
should also be retained to meet statutory and contractual requirements, and those of the Data and AI
Ethics Framework.[^src-govs-010-section-6-7]

**Ask before the work starts, not at sign-off.** Information governance advice, and the corporate
data protection impact assessment process, sit with the information governance function, and
[who to ask](r3-who-to-ask.qmd) is the route to them. Go there while the question is
still what data to use, because a data protection impact assessment raised after the analysis is
built is a review of a decision already taken.

This playbook does not restate the DPIA process. It is a corporate process that applies to more than
analysis, and a second version of it here would go stale the first time it changed.

[^src-govs-010-section-5-3]: GovS 010 section 5.3
